extracted.intended_audience: Recipients of Title IX obligations (postsecondary institutions, elementary and secondary schools), Title IX Coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, institutional administrators, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_short: defining Title IX education program scope
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying when and how Title IX applies to sexual harassment (including on-campus, off-campus, online, and student-organization-controlled locations), what constitutes a complainant/respondent, training and posting requirements for Title IX personnel, and dismissal/disciplinary options available to recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education program or activity includes locations/events/circumstances under recipient's substantial control and student-organization buildings
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(a) revised to state that “education program or activity” includes locations, events, or circumstances over which the recipient exercised substantial control over both the respondent and the context in which the harassment occurs, and also includes any building owned or controlled by a student organization that is officially recognized by a postsecondary institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that Title IX coverage is not strictly geographic; examples include buildings within campus on land owned by the institution that are rented to a recognized student organization. Note: this phrasing is not the same as the Clery Act's “noncampus building or property.” Whether off-campus incidents fall under Title IX is a fact-specific inquiry tied to whether the recipient exercised substantial control over the respondent and context. Recipients must consider their own operations when applying this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complainant definition and formal-complaint participation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: “Complainant” is defined as “an individual who is alleged to be the victim of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment.” However, to file a formal complaint the complainant must be “participating in or attempting to participate in” the recipient's education program or activity at the time the formal complaint is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the broad protection of the statute (no restriction on identity of complainant) but limits who can initiate a formal Title IX grievance to those with current or attempted participation in the program. Recipients are still required to respond promptly and non-deliberately-indifferently to complainants even if they do not meet formal-complaint standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent definition unrestricted by affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Respondent” is defined as “an individual who has been reported to be the perpetrator of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment” without restricting a respondent to being enrolled or employed by the recipient or having any other affiliation or connection with the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means alleged perpetrators can be non-affiliates; jurisdictional application still requires analysis under the “education program or activity” standard (substantial control, context). Recipients may have limited disciplinary authority over non-affiliates and may exercise discretion accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory dismissal for allegations outside education program or activity (but other action permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(3)(i) revised to expressly provide that a mandatory dismissal of allegations in a formal complaint about conduct not occurring in the recipient's education program or activity is “for purposes of title IX or [34 CFR part 106]; such a dismissal does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an allegation does not occur in the education program or activity, the recipient must dismiss for Title IX purposes, but may still address the conduct under other institutional policies or codes of conduct. The dismissal is jurisdictional, not a bar to institutional discipline or supportive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary dismissal when respondent no longer enrolled/employed
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(3)(ii) provides that a recipient may in its discretion dismiss a formal complaint if the respondent is no longer enrolled or employed by the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges that completing a full Title IX grievance process may be impractical when the recipient lacks disciplinary authority over the respondent; recipients retain discretion to dismiss but still must ensure prompt, non-deliberately indifferent responses (e.g., provide supportive measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may address conduct outside Title IX via their own policies/processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the final regulations prohibits a recipient from resolving allegations of conduct outside the recipient's education program or activity by applying the same grievance process required under §106.45 for formal complaints of Title IX sexual harassment, even though such a process would not be required under Title IX or these final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients retain discretion to investigate or discipline off-program conduct under institutional codes of conduct, and are encouraged to offer supportive measures to affected individuals regardless of Title IX jurisdiction. They are not required to separate or ‘‘extricate’’ off-campus conduct from on-campus conduct if facts are intertwined.

rubrics_metrics.name: No geographic test; on-campus vs off-campus is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Final regulations do not impose a geographic test or draw a distinction between on-campus misconduct and off-campus misconduct; whether conduct occurs in a recipient's education program or activity does not necessarily depend on the geographic location of the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Application depends on statutory/regulatory definitions of “program or activity” and the “substantial control” standard. Examples: teacher conduct that affects the educational environment may be within the program though it occurred off-campus; student-organization-controlled buildings can be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement on scope of education program or activity and posting training materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Title IX Coordinator, investigator, decision-maker, and person who facilitates an informal resolution process must be trained on (among other things) “the scope of the recipient's education program or activity.” Section 106.45(b)(10)(i)(D) revised so that materials used to train Title IX personnel must be posted on a recipient's website (or made available for inspection if no website).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures transparency so students, employees, and the public understand the scope of Title IX coverage at a recipient. Training must include how to assess whether conduct falls within the recipient's program or activity (substantial control/context analysis). If recipient lacks a website, materials must be available for public inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online/digital harassment covered if within program or activity; operations may include recipient-owned/operated networks
rubrics_metrics.description: Education program or activity jurisdictional condition is a fact-specific inquiry; the statutory/regulatory definitions of “program or activity” encompass “all of the operations of” recipients, which may include computer and internet networks, digital platforms, and computer hardware or software owned or operated by, or used in the operations of, the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual harassment perpetrated via cell phones or the internet is covered if it occurred in the recipient's education program or activity (e.g., student uses personal device to harass during class). The final regs do not make coverage contingent on the method of perpetration. Even where Title IX does not require action, recipients may still address online misconduct under their own policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of Gebser/Davis framework: actual knowledge and deliberate indifference; hostile environment standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations adopt and adapt the Gebser/Davis framework of actual knowledge and deliberate indifference and utilize the Supreme Court's interpretation in Davis that sexual harassment actionable under Title IX is conduct “so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively denies a person equal access to education.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the substantive filter for Title IX liability: (1) harassment must meet the severity/pervasiveness/objective-offensiveness standard; (2) recipient must have actual knowledge and be deliberately indifferent to be liable. Training and fact-specific analyses should incorporate these legal standards when deciding whether to investigate or adjudicate under Title IX.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must respond promptly and in a non-deliberately indifferent manner to persons alleging sexual harassment
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient with actual knowledge of sexual harassment in the recipient's education program or activity must respond pursuant to §106.44(a); any individual alleged to be a victim of conduct that could constitute sexual harassment is a “complainant” to whom the recipient must respond in a prompt, non-deliberately indifferent manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty applies regardless of the complainant's affiliation/identity; it includes offering supportive measures and determining whether to initiate a formal grievance. Timeliness and substantive responsiveness are necessary to avoid deliberate indifference. Even complaints about conduct outside the program may warrant supportive measures or other institutional action.
